source.title: PLUME: Building a Network-Native Foundation Model for Wireless Traces via Protocol-Aware Tokenization
source.authors: Swadhin Pradhan; Shazal Irshad; Jerome Henry

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study varies model size and reports next-packet prediction accuracy, offering a different-measure test of whether performance changes predictably with scale. It does not measure held-out cross-entropy or fit scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The paper cites compute-optimal scaling work and says its larger-model accuracy drop is consistent with overfitting under those laws. Those cited results are not rows. The relevant original result here is the paper's own model-size comparison in Table 6; other reported results do not test the listed scaling versions.
record.test_reason: The only size comparison (Table 6) is a three-width model-selection sweep, framed as finding 'the compute-optimal operating point'. All three models share one fixed 48.9M-token corpus trained for 20 epochs, so data is the bottleneck. It reports token accuracy on the pretraining task (next-packet prediction), not held-out loss. It fits no scaling law and varies no compute or token allocation, and next-packet accuracy is the pretraining objective, not a downstream task. The paper cites Hoffmann and Kaplan only to explain why the 450M model does worse. None of these results bears on whether any version holds.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors frame the width sweep as finding a compute-optimal operating point. Medium (225M) is best, and they attribute the Large model's drop to overfitting the 48.9M-token corpus, citing Hoffmann and Kaplan on parameter–data imbalance. The paper's main conclusions concern tokenizer, data curation and parity with frontier LLMs, not scaling.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares three widths and parameter counts on the same corpus and reports token accuracy; it does not fit held-out cross-entropy power laws or vary compute-optimal parameter/token allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: Model size changes the reported accuracy: the 225M model outperforms both the 140M and 450M models. The authors attribute the largest model's drop to possible overfitting on the available corpus.

fits_no_version.finding: At fixed data (48.9M tokens, 20 epochs) and fixed iterations, next-packet token accuracy is non-monotonic in width: 140M 0.903, 225M 0.927, 450M 0.801. Field accuracy follows the same pattern (0.884, 0.922, 0.780).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In a small, repeated-data regime, increasing model size beyond a point degrades pretraining-task accuracy (overfitting), rather than improving it smoothly.

record.problems: The scaling comparison covers only three model sizes on one fixed corpus and reports token accuracy rather than held-out loss. No uncertainty is stated for the Table 6 size comparison; the paper itself notes that the 450M model may overfit the 48.9M-token corpus.
record.rows_left_out: No other rows bearing on the tested version were left out. Other reported metrics and cited scaling results do not test a listed version.

untested.parts: No held-out loss or power-law fit; only three sizes, all data-limited.
No fit on small runs or extrapolation.
No fixed-compute sweep over parameters and tokens; tokens are held fixed.
Depth is fixed and only width varies, so parameter count is not held fixed.
Wireless-trace modality, but no power-law form is fitted.
No downstream task is measured across scale; anomaly detection and RCA are reported only for the 140M model.
No exponents or allocations are fitted or compared.

record.verdict_notes: Downgraded from 'tests/T2' because the size sweep is a data-bottlenecked selection exercise measuring pretraining-task accuracy. That fits neither V1 (which requires loss with data not the bottleneck) nor V6 (which requires downstream tasks). Table 6 accuracy values are inconsistent with Tables 2 and 9 for the same 140M model, and the evaluation set is unstated.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss or power-law fit over parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run fit or extrapolation to larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep over parameter and token counts, or fitted compute-optimal trend.
No comparison of architecture details at fixed parameter count.
The study uses wireless traces, but does not test whether the same power-law loss form holds in that modality or under other training regimes.
The size comparison reports next-packet token accuracy, not downstream-task performance across scale or performance as a function of pretraining loss.
No scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocations are fitted or compared across fitting choices.

The Small model's 0.903 here also differs from the 0.831 in Table 2 and the per-category values in Table 9; the evaluation set for Table 6 is not stated.
